compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Picture a regional office with one distributor's display photos, three months of branch shipments, stock and returns records, and a rebate contract spread on the table. Both are asked the same question: these three lines are not selling, what happens next.

Both will probably go through the papers, and both will ask where the numbers came from. The shared S gives them an interest in facts that can be compared, and the shared P makes both willing to keep some room to adjust as new information arrives. Checking shop displays and sales figures can illustrate their shared Sensing preference. Either person may find practical solutions, and neither the records they open nor their willingness to adjust a plan tells you how they will make the decision.

The divergence comes at the judging step. Facing the same matter, one more often asks what this arrangement means for the people in the store and who carries the cost; the other more often asks whether this holds under one standard, and which link does not match. Both questions move things forward, and both miss something.

### The same stock data, two weighings

In the fictional stock review, two staff members sit down with the distributor. The material is identical and so is the authority — either may propose a trial, changing a display needs the store manager's consent, and adjusting a rebate has to go to a supervisor. There is one question: what happens to these three lines next, and under what conditions this step counts as working.

One approach weighs the effects of a trial on the store team and its customers. It asks whether a week of extra work would overload a two-person shift or leave customers with less help.

Another approach asks whether the same eligibility and success criteria could apply across comparable stores. Either approach can use the same sales records, and either person could apply both sets of criteria.

Both will raise the same three possibilities — insufficient promotion, a distribution structure problem, the product itself not fitting — and differ in which one each would rather test first, and at what cost. Staff may see an unsupported trial as extra work, and the distributor may hear unexplained questions as distrust. Those costs have nothing to do with type and everything to do with who holds the authority and who usually deals with this store.

Who speaks first, and which document is asked for first, cannot type anyone. Someone who has worked channels for years, of either type, will ask for the shipment detail first; an ISTP taking this over for the first time may stand in the store for a while to see how the goods are actually placed. Role, experience, deadline and information all rewrite the order.

In the common four-function notation used here, ESFP is Se–Fi–Te–Ni and ISTP is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. Only two processes share a name, Se and Ni, and neither sits in the same slot: Se is first for ESFP and second for ISTP; Ni is fourth for ESFP and third for ISTP.

The judging processes do not correspond one to one either. ESFP has Fi second and Te third; ISTP has Ti first and Fe fourth. So this is neither "Fi swapped for Fe and Te for Ti" in place, nor "the perceiving side unchanged, only the judging swapped" — the two judging processes carry different weight and different positions in each arrangement.

The arrangement describes an emphasis under one dynamics convention only. It does not establish who acts first, whose words are harder, or who is better at which kind of work. Nor does it explain whether the two would describe the same scene the same way: how detailed a description is depends on where someone stood, how long they watched, and whether anyone was taking notes for them.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables: for ESFP's Te and ISTP's Ni, some versions give only the function name without settling an attitude. When a version differs, check whether it cites a source, then read the first two positions for this pair. compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: the two passages below are editorial fictions about a distribution channel, covering the organisation of information and ways of communicating only, and corresponding to no real distributor or person. The numbers appear only to make the accounting checkable and represent no actual trading situation.

### The distributor says "it is not that I do not push, it genuinely does not sell"

(Fictional scene.) At the month-end count, two thousand units sit in the distributor's warehouse, and three lines account for seventy per cent of it. As the sentence is said, both hold the same material: display photos of the three lines, branch shipments for the last three months, opening and closing stock, returns records, and a rebate contract that has not yet expired.

The decision question is the same: what to do next, and by what condition to judge that it worked. Three lines not selling may mean nobody pushes them, that they were placed in stores that cannot sell them, or that the product does not fit — all three are testable hypotheses, and either type may back one first.

In this fictional example, one line of inquiry checks the display, price tags and whether the store team can take on the extra work. The proposal is something the store can agree to now, such as moving two lines to the entrance for a week. The risk is overstepping: changing a display without the manager's consent makes the other person feel ordered about.

Another line of inquiry checks whether shipments are concentrated in a few stores, where the stock and sales figures diverge, and whether the same trial criteria can apply to comparable stores. Either person could pursue both lines of inquiry. The risk is that the other person feels audited: a run of questions easily has the distributor hear the checking as distrust.

A workable verification splits "not selling" into accounts that can be reconciled: by the same store and the same SKU, reconcile opening stock with closing stock using receipts, sales, returns and transfers for the same period. Check whether returns or transfers are already included in net figures before counting them separately; then, by the basis agreed in advance, compare closing stock with sales for the same period, listing stores and SKUs with zero sales separately. Stock that does not reconcile and stock that is simply high are two different problems with different paths — the first needs the record gap found, the second is where structure gets discussed. Whether the rebate is adjusted follows the contract terms and approval authority, and is not tied directly to the result of the check.

Both types can run this check; the difference is only which kind of reason is cited more often once the result is in: whether the store can carry this week, or whether the conclusion holds across all stores.

### A cousin wants to stock your product in a county-town shop

(Fictional scene.) A cousin runs a hardware shop in a county town, about twenty square metres, and wants to stock your product, starting with a few cases. Both hear the same set of information: the shop's size and position, the number of similar shops nearby, the monthly turnover he reports, how many lines he plans to carry, and the minimum order and return terms he can accept. There are gaps in the information, and they are the same gaps.

There is also one decision question: whether to give this small minimum order a chance, and on what conditions.

ESFP more often weighs the person: what neighbours buy when they come in, how he deals with people, whether a few cases would become a burden in his shop. ISTP more often weighs the conditions: whether the density of similar shops and his turnover can support one line, and whether the minimum order and return terms are the same for a relative as for other customers.

Both reasons hold, and both can go wrong: reading the person can misjudge, and reading the numbers can be misled by self-reported turnover. Either type may give the chance because "this man knows his trade and the position is right", and either may decline because "there are already too many similar shops on this street".

So "does the reason contain numbers" cannot separate them. A sentence with numbers may come from any preference, and so may a purely descriptive one. What discriminates better is, in front of the same gaps, which standard each finally adopts and who has the authority to decide it.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread is taking ISTP's few words as coldness. How much someone says depends on the occasion, familiarity, role and energy at the time, with no stable correspondence to four letters. ISTP may spend a whole day with a store, and may talk a great deal at a dinner table; ESFP may equally have nothing to say on a particular visit. Explaining politeness or warmth through function positions gets both wrong at once.

The second is taking ESFP's warmth as social technique, or, conversely, taking F as only maintaining relationships. The F side of a judgement includes people and relationships, and also fairness, promises and who has been left out; an ESFP may insist on keeping a share for the weakest store when allocating goods, and the reason is not a personal friendship. Reducing F to "being nice" makes that kind of judgement invisible.

The third slip is treating "can they do the numbers" as a type label. Anyone who works a channel calculates stock-to-sales ratios, and anyone who has run a store looks at the display first; that is training. The difference between T and F is not whether the arithmetic happens but which standard is finally adopted: a rule that can be applied consistently, or what this means for specific people.

The numbers appear only to make the accounting checkable and represent no actual trading situation.
### The distributor says "it is not that I do not push, it genuinely does not sell"

(Fictional scene.) At the month-end count, two thousand units sit in the distributor's warehouse, and three lines account for seventy per cent of it. As the sentence is said, both hold the same material: display photos of the three lines, branch shipments for the last three months, opening and closing stock, returns records, and a rebate contract that has not yet expired.

The decision question is the same: what to do next, and by what condition to judge that it worked. Three lines not selling may mean nobody pushes them, that they were placed in stores that cannot sell them, or that the product does not fit — all three are testable hypotheses, and either type may back one first.

In this fictional example, one line of inquiry checks the display, price tags and whether the store team can take on the extra work. The proposal is something the store can agree to now, such as moving two lines to the entrance for a week. The risk is overstepping: changing a display without the manager's consent makes the other person feel ordered about.

Another line of inquiry checks whether shipments are concentrated in a few stores, where the stock and sales figures diverge, and whether the same trial criteria can apply to comparable stores. Either person could pursue both lines of inquiry. The risk is that the other person feels audited: a run of questions easily has the distributor hear the checking as distrust.

A workable verification splits "not selling" into accounts that can be reconciled: by the same store and the same SKU, reconcile opening stock with closing stock using receipts, sales, returns and transfers for the same period. Check whether returns or transfers are already included in net figures before counting them separately; then, by the basis agreed in advance, compare closing stock with sales for the same period, listing stores and SKUs with zero sales separately. Stock that does not reconcile and stock that is simply high are two different problems with different paths — the first needs the record gap found, the second is where structure gets discussed. Whether the rebate is adjusted follows the contract terms and approval authority, and is not tied directly to the result of the check.

Both types can run this check; the difference is only which kind of reason is cited more often once the result is in: whether the store can carry this week, or whether the conclusion holds across all stores.
### A cousin wants to stock your product in a county-town shop

(Fictional scene.) A cousin runs a hardware shop in a county town, about twenty square metres, and wants to stock your product, starting with a few cases. Both hear the same set of information: the shop's size and position, the number of similar shops nearby, the monthly turnover he reports, how many lines he plans to carry, and the minimum order and return terms he can accept. There are gaps in the information, and they are the same gaps.
There is also one decision question: whether to give this small minimum order a chance, and on what conditions.

ESFP more often weighs the person: what neighbours buy when they come in, how he deals with people, whether a few cases would become a burden in his shop. ISTP more often weighs the conditions: whether the density of similar shops and his turnover can support one line, and whether the minimum order and return terms are the same for a relative as for other customers.

Both reasons hold, and both can go wrong: reading the person can misjudge, and reading the numbers can be misled by self-reported turnover. Either type may give the chance because "this man knows his trade and the position is right", and either may decline because "there are already too many similar shops on this street".

So "does the reason contain numbers" cannot separate them. A sentence with numbers may come from any preference, and so may a purely descriptive one. What discriminates better is, in front of the same gaps, which standard each finally adopts and who has the authority to decide it.

body: The first misread is taking ISTP's few words as coldness. How much someone says depends on the occasion, familiarity, role and energy at the time, with no stable correspondence to four letters. ISTP may spend a whole day with a store, and may talk a great deal at a dinner table; ESFP may equally have nothing to say on a particular visit. Explaining politeness or warmth through function positions gets both wrong at once.

The second is taking ESFP's warmth as social technique, or, conversely, taking F as only maintaining relationships. The F side of a judgement includes people and relationships, and also fairness, promises and who has been left out; an ESFP may insist on keeping a share for the weakest store when allocating goods, and the reason is not a personal friendship. Reducing F to "being nice" makes that kind of judgement invisible.

The third slip is treating "can they do the numbers" as a type label. Anyone who works a channel calculates stock-to-sales ratios, and anyone who has run a store looks at the display first; that is training. The difference between T and F is not whether the arithmetic happens but which standard is finally adopted: a rule that can be applied consistently, or what this means for specific people.

items.question: ISTP will also give way for a relationship, and ESFP will also argue with data?

items.answer:
Not by type. A visit usually has two parts: getting the other person willing to keep working together, and letting them know which conditions cannot be vague; both need a specific person to do them, and either type can do either well.

A steadier arrangement divides by experience, authority and what each person wants: whoever knows this store talks about willingness to cooperate; whoever knows the contract and settlement basis checks the conditions; and agree in advance when and how a disagreement over the data gets raised. items.question: Facing a distributor, which half should each handle?

items.answer:
The usual convenient split: one runs the interview and records store feedback, the other checks the data against one basis. The first draws out what the manager says, the second reconciles shipments, stock and returns.

This division has to be stated in advance, or an awkward scene follows: one is building rapport with the manager while the other points out on the spot that the data is wrong, and the atmosphere drops immediately. Agreeing a signal — note it now, compare it outside — removes most of the friction; who takes which part depends on who knows this store and who knows the settlement terms, and swapping is common.

body: Picture a regional office with one distributor's display photos, three months of branch shipments, stock and returns records, and a rebate contract spread on the table. Both are asked the same question: these three lines are not selling, what happens next.

The divergence comes at the judging step. Facing the same matter, one more often asks what this arrangement means for the people in the store and who carries the cost; the other more often asks whether this holds under one standard, and which link does not match. Both questions move things forward, and both miss something.

In the fictional stock review, two staff members sit down with the distributor. One approach weighs the effects of a trial on the store team and its customers. It asks whether a week of extra work would overload a two-person shift or leave customers with less help.

Another approach asks whether the same eligibility and success criteria could apply across comparable stores. Either approach can use the same sales records, and either person could apply both sets of criteria.

Both will raise the same three possibilities — insufficient promotion, a distribution structure problem, the product itself not fitting — and differ in which one each would rather test first, and at what cost. Staff may see an unsupported trial as extra work, and the distributor may hear unexplained questions as distrust. Those costs have nothing to do with type and everything to do with who holds the authority and who usually deals with this store.

Who speaks first, and which document is asked for first, cannot type anyone. sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Picture a regional office with one distributor's display photos, three months of branch shipments, stock and returns records, and a rebate contract spread on the table. Both are asked the same question: these three lines are not selling, what happens next.

Both will probably go through the papers, and both will ask where the numbers came from. The shared S gives them an interest in facts that can be compared, and the shared P makes both willing to keep some room to adjust as new information arrives. Checking shop displays and sales figures can illustrate their shared Sensing preference. Either person may find practical solutions, and neither the records they open nor their willingness to adjust a plan tells you how they will make the decision.

The divergence comes at the judging step. Facing the same matter, one more often asks what this arrangement means for the people in the store and who carries the cost; the other more often asks whether this holds under one standard, and which link does not match. Both questions move things forward, and both miss something.

### The same stock data, two weighings

In the fictional stock review, two staff members sit down with the distributor. The material is identical and so is the authority — either may propose a trial, changing a display needs the store manager's consent, and adjusting a rebate has to go to a supervisor. There is one question: what happens to these three lines next, and under what conditions this step counts as working.

One approach weighs the effects of a trial on the store team and its customers. It asks whether a week of extra work would overload a two-person shift or leave customers with less help.

Another approach asks whether the same eligibility and success criteria could apply across comparable stores. Either approach can use the same sales records, and either person could apply both sets of criteria.

Both will raise the same three possibilities — insufficient promotion, a distribution structure problem, the product itself not fitting — and differ in which one each would rather test first, and at what cost. Staff may see an unsupported trial as extra work, and the distributor may hear unexplained questions as distrust. Those costs have nothing to do with type and everything to do with who holds the authority and who usually deals with this store.

Who speaks first, and which document is asked for first, cannot type anyone. Someone who has worked channels for years, of either type, will ask for the shipment detail first; an ISTP taking this over for the first time may stand in the store for a while to see how the goods are actually placed. Role, experience, deadline and information all rewrite the order.

### Why Se and Ni are shared while the judging processes sit at opposite ends

In the common four-function notation used here, ESFP is Se–Fi–Te–Ni and ISTP is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe. Only two processes share a name, Se and Ni, and neither sits in the same slot: Se is first for ESFP and second for ISTP; Ni is fourth for ESFP and third for ISTP.

The judging processes do not correspond one to one either. ESFP has Fi second and Te third; ISTP has Ti first and Fe fourth. So this is neither "Fi swapped for Fe and Te for Ti" in place, nor "the perceiving side unchanged, only the judging swapped" — the two judging processes carry different weight and different positions in each arrangement.

The arrangement describes an emphasis under one dynamics convention only. It does not establish who acts first, whose words are harder, or who is better at which kind of work. Nor does it explain whether the two would describe the same scene the same way: how detailed a description is depends on where someone stood, how long they watched, and whether anyone was taking notes for them.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables: for ESFP's Te and ISTP's Ni, some versions give only the function name without settling an attitude. When a version differs, check whether it cites a source, then read the first two positions for this pair. Both base pages are the [ESFP profile](/en/personality/esfp) and the [ISTP profile](/en/personality/istp).

Scope note: the two passages below are editorial fictions about a distribution channel, covering the organisation of information and ways of communicating only, and corresponding to no real distributor or person. The numbers appear only to make the accounting checkable and represent no actual trading situation.

### The distributor says "it is not that I do not push, it genuinely does not sell"

(Fictional scene.) At the month-end count, two thousand units sit in the distributor's warehouse, and three lines account for seventy per cent of it. As the sentence is said, both hold the same material: display photos of the three lines, branch shipments for the last three months, opening and closing stock, returns records, and a rebate contract that has not yet expired.

The decision question is the same: what to do next, and by what condition to judge that it worked. Three lines not selling may mean nobody pushes them, that they were placed in stores that cannot sell them, or that the product does not fit — all three are testable hypotheses, and either type may back one first.

In this fictional example, one line of inquiry checks the display, price tags and whether the store team can take on the extra work. The proposal is something the store can agree to now, such as moving two lines to the entrance for a week. The risk is overstepping: changing a display without the manager's consent makes the other person feel ordered about.

Another line of inquiry checks whether shipments are concentrated in a few stores, where the stock and sales figures diverge, and whether the same trial criteria can apply to comparable stores. Either person could pursue both lines of inquiry. The risk is that the other person feels audited: a run of questions easily has the distributor hear the checking as distrust.

A workable verification splits "not selling" into accounts that can be reconciled: by the same store and the same SKU, reconcile opening stock with closing stock using receipts, sales, returns and transfers for the same period. Check whether returns or transfers are already included in net figures before counting them separately; then, by the basis agreed in advance, compare closing stock with sales for the same period, listing stores and SKUs with zero sales separately. Stock that does not reconcile and stock that is simply high are two different problems with different paths — the first needs the record gap found, the second is where structure gets discussed. Whether the rebate is adjusted follows the contract terms and approval authority, and is not tied directly to the result of the check.

Both types can run this check; the difference is only which kind of reason is cited more often once the result is in: whether the store can carry this week, or whether the conclusion holds across all stores.

### A cousin wants to stock your product in a county-town shop

(Fictional scene.) A cousin runs a hardware shop in a county town, about twenty square metres, and wants to stock your product, starting with a few cases. Both hear the same set of information: the shop's size and position, the number of similar shops nearby, the monthly turnover he reports, how many lines he plans to carry, and the minimum order and return terms he can accept. There are gaps in the information, and they are the same gaps.

There is also one decision question: whether to give this small minimum order a chance, and on what conditions.

ESFP more often weighs the person: what neighbours buy when they come in, how he deals with people, whether a few cases would become a burden in his shop. ISTP more often weighs the conditions: whether the density of similar shops and his turnover can support one line, and whether the minimum order and return terms are the same for a relative as for other customers.

Both reasons hold, and both can go wrong: reading the person can misjudge, and reading the numbers can be misled by self-reported turnover. Either type may give the chance because "this man knows his trade and the position is right", and either may decline because "there are already too many similar shops on this street".

So "does the reason contain numbers" cannot separate them. A sentence with numbers may come from any preference, and so may a purely descriptive one. What discriminates better is, in front of the same gaps, which standard each finally adopts and who has the authority to decide it.

sections.body_md:
The first misread is taking ISTP's few words as coldness. How much someone says depends on the occasion, familiarity, role and energy at the time, with no stable correspondence to four letters. ISTP may spend a whole day with a store, and may talk a great deal at a dinner table; ESFP may equally have nothing to say on a particular visit. Explaining politeness or warmth through function positions gets both wrong at once.

The second is taking ESFP's warmth as social technique, or, conversely, taking F as only maintaining relationships. The F side of a judgement includes people and relationships, and also fairness, promises and who has been left out; an ESFP may insist on keeping a share for the weakest store when allocating goods, and the reason is not a personal friendship. Reducing F to "being nice" makes that kind of judgement invisible.

The third slip is treating "can they do the numbers" as a type label. Anyone who works a channel calculates stock-to-sales ratios, and anyone who has run a store looks at the display first; that is training. The difference between T and F is not whether the arithmetic happens but which standard is finally adopted: a rule that can be applied consistently, or what this means for specific people.

When two results differ, check the item bank first: the same questionnaire, language version and scoring convention; if it reports dimension scores, look at whether E/I and T/F both sit near the boundary. Being near a boundary only means those two are sensitive to changes in your answers, not that two complete types both hold.
